    obsy[i] ~ dnorm(ya[i], sd = erry[i])

  beta ~ dnorm(0.0,sd=100)

HK, I've taken a look at your model.  Fortunately there were no serious errors here, it just boiled down to improper model initialization.

I've added initial values for mt, ya, y.norm, and y.scat.  Everything works fine now, and I've taken your model through to building, compiling, and running an MCMC.

See the modified code below.  Please look through the code for comments beginning with "DT", which give a few more details.

Let us know if you have any more questions!

Cheers,
Daniel
NIMBLE development team

library(nimble)

dat <- read.csv("3He3Hedat.csv")

re <- as.numeric(dat$lab) # Change the label to a numeric vector

## Note that the numbers are assigned by "sorting" the labels in alphabetical order

Nre <- length(unique(dat$lab))
## Unique removes duplicated vector, we want to know how many groups of
## data are there

N <- nrow(dat) # Total No of data sets
obsy <- dat$S    # Response variable in MeV
obsx <-  dat$E   # Predictors
erry <- dat$Stat # Error in MeV
set <- dat$lab # Get the labels as a vector

## Inputting the quoted systematic uncertainty:
syst = c(log(1.057),log(1.082),log(1.037),log(1.045),log(1.038))
                                        ## In accordance to
                                        ## 1 Bon99 5.7%
                                        ## 2 Daw71 8.2%
                                        ## 3 Jun98 3.7%
                                        ## 4 Kra87 4.5%
                                        ## 5 Kud04 3.8%

samplerCode <-  nimbleCode({
    for (i in 1:N) {
        mut[i] <- (exp(2.429819509 * i.screen * (obsx[i]^(-1.5)))) * (alpha + beta * obsx[i] + gamma * (obsx[i]^2))
        yt[i] <- y.norm[re[i]]*mut[i]

        ## Temp mean (mut) multiplied by normalising constant,

        ya[i] ~ dnorm(yt[i],sd = y.scat[re[i]])

        ## re[i] refers to the index that we would use to refer to the category

        obsy[i] ~ dnorm(ya[i], sd = erry[i])

        ## Propagating the errors in observations of y

    }
    ## PRIORS
    ## polynomial parameters
    alpha ~ T(dnorm(0.0,sd=100),0,Inf)

    ## Note the difference in how we truncate the distributions

    beta ~ dnorm(0.0,sd=100)
    gamma ~ dnorm(0.0,sd=100)
    i.screen ~ T(dnorm(0.0,sd=100),0,Inf)

    ## Some sort of hyperprior for the "grand mean"

    mt ~ T(dnorm(0.0,sd=5),0,Inf)
    for (k in 1:Nre){

        ## Systematic Uncertainty as a highly informative prior
        y.norm[k] ~ dlnorm(0,sd = syst[k])       ## DT: changed log(1.0) to 0

        y.scat[k] ~ T(dnorm(mt,sd=100),0,Inf)
    }
})

samplerData <- list(obsy = obsy)    # Response variable

samplerConst <- list(N = N, # Sample size
                     Nre = Nre,
                     re = re, # This is used to "iterate")
                     erry = erry,

                     syst = syst,
                     obsx = obsx     # Predictors   ## DT: moved predictor/covariate obsx to "constants",
                                                    ## more appropriate than "data", although if you plan
                                                    ## on ever changing the values of obsx, then move it back to "data"

                     )

samplerInits <- list(alpha = 1,
                     beta = -1,
                     gamma = 1,

                     i.screen = 1e-6,
                     mt = 1,                  ## DT: initial value added
                     ya = rep(1, N),          ## DT: initial value added
                     y.norm = rep(1, Nre),    ## DT: initial value added
                     y.scat = rep(1, Nre)     ## DT: initial value added
                     )

ourmodel <- nimbleModel(samplerCode, samplerConst, samplerData, samplerInits)

Rmodel <- ourmodel

Rmodel$calculate()     ## DT: -34550.91  good, a real number.  model is now fully initialized

conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)
conf$printSamplers(byType = TRUE)
conf$printMonitors()
Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)

Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

set.seed(0)
samples <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, 10000)

library(basicMCMCplots)
samplesPlot(samples, c('alpha', 'beta', 'gamma'))
samplesPlot(samples, 'y.norm')

samplesSummary(samples)

I just got a new laptop, and when I tried to compile a model, I got an error Failed to create shared library:

In system(cmd) : 'make' not found

I then realized that my IT tech had not installed Rtools, so I installed Rtools35. The problem persisted (even after a reboot), so I thought maybe I needed Rtools34 instead. I installed it (but it failed to update the Windows registry - not sure if that is a problem), but still no luck compiling.
Running the following code suggest that R 3.5.0 (the latest version I am authorized to install) needs Rtools35.

Hi HK,

In the type declaration system, "double(D)" means there will be D indices.  If you want a vector of length 100000, you would use "x = double(1)" to indicate x will be one-dimensional in the sense of taking one index.  If xout is also a vector then "xout = double(1)" is correct.  But if xout is a scalar, you want "xout = double(0)".  The same goes for the returnType.  You haven't shown how you are trying to use myapproxR, so I can't tell what you intend.

As you note, another option would be to write what you need as a nimbleFunction, which will give faster performance.

-Perry

messages.subject_clean: user-defined distribution based on CDF of multivariate Gaussian
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to the developers and countless contributors for all the great work building this useful software.

I am attempting to fit a model for jointly dependent binary response vectors (e.g., presence/absence of multiple species at a site). The model is based on a latent multivariate Gaussian distribution of the same dimension as the binary data vector, where realizations of the binary process arise as element-wise truncations above (success) or below (failure) zero. I have been able to develop an MCMC algorithm for this model using NIMBLE for the case when the latent multivariate Gaussian variables are updated with the rest of the parameters. The approach is analogous to a multivariate Albert and Chib (1993) probit model. However, the MCMC algorithm is, unsurprisingly, inefficient. I would like to try integrating out the latent multivariate Gaussian variables. This involves computing CDFs of multivariate Gaussian distributions with general covariance matrices, which I don't believe is currently supported with base NIMBLE functions. Thus, I am trying to write my own custom distributions for the binary response vectors, relying on existing R packages (tmvtnorm or TruncatedNormal) to do the CDF evaluations. I am using nimbleRcall() to try and make the function pmvnorm() from tmvtnorm available to use in my custom probability distribution. Unfortunately, I get an error when I try to build the nimble model, although the custom density function and sampler I defined appear to work fine when I test them out. The error appears to come from a check within pmvnorm().

A toy example of the hierarchical model is shown below. This should reproduce the error I get (Error in checkmvArgs(lower = lower, upper = upper, mean = mean, corr = corr, : ‘lower’ not specified or contains NA). However, as I mentioned above, I think the error is probably coming from the pmvnorm() function, not NIMBLE. I suspect that my issue comes from the way I am trying to use pmvnorm() via nimbleRcall + nimbleFunction. Any insight into this issue would be super helpful.

Thanks!
--Henry

library(nimble); library(tmvtnorm)
## define multivariate probit function ----
mvprobit <- function(z, mu, sigma, log = 0){
  lb <- z
  ub <- z
  lb[z == 0] <- -Inf
  lb[z == 1] <- 0
  ub[z == 0] <- 0
  ub[z == 1] <- Inf
  as.numeric(pmvnorm(mean = mu, sigma = sigma, lower = lb, upper = ub))
}
## nimble-ize mvprobit ----
nimble_mvprobit <-
  nimbleRcall(prototype = function(z = double(1), mu = double(1),
                                   sigma = double(2), log = integer(0, default = 0)){},
              Rfun = 'mvprobit',
              returnType = double(0))
## define multivariate bernoulli based on multivariate Gaussian ----
dmbern <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = double(1), mu = double(1), sigma = double(2),
                 log = integer(0, default = 0)) {
    returnType(double(0))
    Prob <- nimble_mvprobit(z = x, mu = mu, sigma = sigma, log = log)
    if(log) return(log(Prob))
    else return(Prob)
  })
rmbern <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(n = integer(0, default = 1), mu = double(1), sigma = double(2)) {

I got a slightly different error, but close enough that I think it's related.  (Have you updated nimble recently?)

The output I get is:

> model <- nimbleModel(code = code, constants = constants, inits = inits)

defining model...
Registering the following user-provided distributions: dmbern .
NIMBLE has registered dmbern as a distribution based on its use in BUGS code. Note that if you make changes to the nimbleFunctions for the distribution, you must call 'deregisterDistributions' before using the distribution in BUGS code for those changes to take effect.
Adding prior_mean, prior_prec, cov as data for building model.
building model...
setting data and initial values...
running calculate on model (any error reports that follow may simply reflect missing values in model variables) ... Error in checkmvArgs(lower = lower, upper = upper, mean = mean, corr = corr,  :
  ‘mean’ is not a numeric vector

checking model sizes and dimensions... This model is not fully initialized. This is not an error. To see which variables are not initialized, use model$initializeInfo(). For more information on model initialization, see help(modelInitialization).
model building finished.

The "any error reports that follow may simply reflect missing values in model variables" is important.  It means you don't necessarily need to worry about the reported error message if it simply results from uninitialized variables.  The function did exit successfully and a model was created.  I following the instructions to do model$initializeInfo() and got the following:

> model$initializeInfo()
Missing values (NAs) or non-finite values were found in model variables: z, means. This is not an error, but some or all variables may need to be initialized for certain algorithms to operate properly. For more information on model initialization, see help(modelInitialization).

So it seems that z and means were not initialized (did you intend to have one variable called "mean" and another called "means"?).

So far, no problems, just incomplete initialization.

I did check to see if your model would compile and note the following:

In rmbern, it won't successfully cast a logical vector to a double vector return type, so please use:

   result <- numeric(length = length(latent), value = latent > 0)
   return(result)

   F is not recognized for FALSE, so please use "prec_param = FALSE"

With those changes I was able to compile the model.  I stopped there.

-Perry

On Mon, Jun 17, 2019 at 4:40 PM Henry Scharf <henryr...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Many thanks to the developers and countless contributors for all the great work building this useful software.
>
> I am attempting to fit a model for jointly dependent binary response vectors (e.g., presence/absence of multiple species at a site). The model is based on a latent multivariate Gaussian distribution of the same dimension as the binary data vector, where realizations of the binary process arise as element-wise truncations above (success) or below (failure) zero. I have been able to develop an MCMC algorithm for this model using NIMBLE for the case when the latent multivariate Gaussian variables are updated with the rest of the parameters. The approach is analogous to a multivariate Albert and Chib (1993) probit model. However, the MCMC algorithm is, unsurprisingly, inefficient. I would like to try integrating out the latent multivariate Gaussian variables. This involves computing CDFs of multivariate Gaussian distributions with general covariance matrices, which I don't believe is currently supported with base NIMBLE functions. Thus, I am trying to write my own custom distributions for the binary response vectors, relying on existing R packages (tmvtnorm or TruncatedNormal) to do the CDF evaluations. I am using nimbleRcall() to try and make the function pmvnorm() from tmvtnorm available to use in my custom probability distribution. Unfortunately, I get an error when I try to build the nimble model, although the custom density function and sampler I defined appear to work fine when I test them out. The error appears to come from a check within pmvnorm().
>
> A toy example of the hierarchical model is shown below. This should reproduce the error I get (Error in checkmvArgs(lower = lower, upper = upper, mean = mean, corr = corr, : ‘lower’ not specified or contains NA). However, as I mentioned above, I think the error is probably coming from the pmvnorm() function, not NIMBLE. I suspect that my issue comes from the way I am trying to use pmvnorm() via nimbleRcall + nimbleFunction. Any insight into this issue would be super helpful.
>
> Thanks!
> --Henry
>
>
> library(nimble); library(tmvtnorm)
> ## define multivariate probit function ----
> mvprobit <- function(z, mu, sigma, log = 0){
>   lb <- z
>   ub <- z
>   lb[z == 0] <- -Inf
>   lb[z == 1] <- 0
>   ub[z == 0] <- 0
>   ub[z == 1] <- Inf
>   as.numeric(pmvnorm(mean = mu, sigma = sigma, lower = lb, upper = ub))
> }
> ## nimble-ize mvprobit ----
> nimble_mvprobit <-
>   nimbleRcall(prototype = function(z = double(1), mu = double(1),
>                                    sigma = double(2), log = integer(0, default = 0)){},
>               Rfun = 'mvprobit',
>               returnType = double(0))
> ## define multivariate bernoulli based on multivariate Gaussian ----
> dmbern <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(x = double(1), mu = double(1), sigma = double(2),
>                  log = integer(0, default = 0)) {
>     returnType(double(0))
>     Prob <- nimble_mvprobit(z = x, mu = mu, sigma = sigma, log = log)
>     if(log) return(log(Prob))
>     else return(Prob)
>   })
> rmbern <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(n = integer(0, default = 1), mu = double(1), sigma = double(2)) {
>     returnType(double(1))
>     chol_mat <- chol(sigma)
>     latent <- rmnorm_chol(n = 1, mean = mu, cholesky = chol_mat, prec_param = F)
>     return(latent > 0)
>   })
> ## define the model ----
> code <- nimbleCode({
>   ## mixture probabilities + response distribution ----
>   mean[1:n_species] ~ dmnorm(mean = prior_mean[1:n_species],
>                              prec = prior_prec[1:n_species, 1:n_species])
>   for(i in 1:n_observations){
>     z[i, 1:n_species] ~ dmbern(mu = means[1:n_species], sigma = cov[1:n_species, 1:n_species])
>   }
> })
> ## constants + inits ----
> n_observations <- 1e2
> n_species <- 2
> constants <- list(
>   n_observations = n_observations,
>   n_species = n_species,
>   prior_mean = rep(0, n_species),
>   prior_prec = diag(n_species),
>   cov = diag(n_species)
> )
> inits <- list(
>   mean = rep(0, n_species)
> )
> ## nimbleModel ----
> model <- nimbleModel(code = code, constants = constants, inits = inits)
>

Many thanks for taking a look!

Henry

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am wondering how well nimble's current PMCMC algorithms are adapted for situations where you want to fit a state space model to data from multiple (N>1) sites. In our case the latent state X is the unobserved density of an insect and N=4 geographical locations.  It is clear that X should be site specific, but also that data from all 4 locations should contribute to estimating (global) model parameters.

So how best to tackle this?

Some options coming to mind include...
1) We could simply declare X1, X2, X3 and X4, one for each of the four sites, and list all four in the latents argument of a PF sampler. But would the current nimble PMCMC algorithm do the right thing?
2) We could simply declare a single latent state of the form X=c(X1, X2, X3, X4) and ensure suitable breaks in the dependence structure.  But would the breaks in conditionality generate algorithmic problems?
3) We could declare RW_PF_block samplers per site, i.e. we would need at least as many samplers as there are sites. But I'm not sure whether or not that would give valid inference.
4) We could write a new sampler that accounts for some current limitation. But do we don't need to?

How would you approach this problem?

Best regards
David

Hi David,

Yes, I think it is possible (although I see our documentation could be more helpful on this).  You'll want to make X a matrix and indicate which dimension indexes time as follows.

The underlying particle filter type (auxiliary or bootstrap) is controlled by the pfType control list entry to RW_PF_block (or RW_PF) (See User Manual section 8.1.2).   Another control list entry, pfControl, is passed as the control list to buildAuxiliaryFilter or buildBootstrapFilter.  The documentation for those describes the timeIndex control list option, which lets you say which dimension of the latent state variable indexes time.

So what you want is the following:
1. Set up X as a matrix, either cbind(X1, X2, X3, X4) or rbind(X1, X2, X3, X4)
2. In RW_PF_block, include control = list(latents = "X", pfType = "auxiliary", pfControl = list(timeIndex = 1 <or 2, depending on how you set it up>), <your other choices>)

For <your other choices>, see that User Manual section, or the source code for full details.

I hope it works!

-Perry

I'm running a a random-effects model using the nimbleMCMC function. The model works fine if the number of units in the data (the number of random effects or nodes) is of normal size (e.g. 500 units), but I get an error message if the number gets huge (e.g. 20000 units).

Therefore, I was wondering whether there is a maximum on the number of nodes that can be specified in the model when using R-Nimble (nimbleMCMC)?   Note also that I am not monitoring these random effects.

Kind regards
Christel
